item.title: The Birds of GTA 6: A Field Guide to Vice City and Leonida's Wildlife (452 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.audubon.org/magazine/birds-of-gta-6-field-guide-vice-city-wildlife, See on Hacker News

From Roseate Spoonbills in the Grassrivers to gulls over Vice Beach, here's what it takes to find Leonida’s birds, how the spotting mechanics work, and what Rockstar’s artists got right.

I finished collecting the bricks of cocaine and landed my bullet-ridden seaplane at the dock. It was time for birdwatching.

A few minutes after midnight on Thursday morning, I joined millions of other gamers for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest in the smash video game series from Rockstar Games. The new installment is already a worldwide sensation, earning more than $1.8 billion in revenue the day it was released. 

Grand Theft Auto, or GTA, games are famous for their “open worlds,” which allow players to explore massive, intricately detailed versions of America. Much of that exploration is focused on mayhem and chaos: The story missions usher players through criminal underworlds, and players are at any time free to steal cars, rob stores and pedestrians, and initiate anarchy. 

But GTA 6 has more going on than just criminality—it’s also a world filled with wildlife. Previous GTA games were set in fictionalized versions of New York City and Hollywood, but the new one returns to Vice City, its version of Miami, which was also the setting for 2002’s installment. Unlike that game, however, GTA 6’s South Florida is complete with dozens of species of birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, mammals, and other creatures. The in-game Progress menu tracks all kinds of items to find, including 338 vehicles, 205 weapons, and, of primary interest to me, at least 60 bird species. 

I made it my mission to find them all as quickly as possible.

(Side note: Pre-release marketing for GTA 6 touted 62 bird species, but the official birds Progress screen only lists 60, with a handful of others listed on the hunting screen.)

I am one hour in and I’ve found 16/60 birds https://t.co/81x42O1BuY

— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026

You begin the game as Jason, a low-level criminal working to raise money to support his young family. You’re equipped with zoom binoculars before the very first mission—tracking drug runners through a swamp and escaping with the seaplane—and I used them immediately, stopping mid-lurk to scan some Double-crested Cormorants on a dock. (Distracted from the job at hand to look at birds—just like real life!) They looked like Double-crested Cormorants! 

After the first mission the player is free to explore the entirety of the map, stealing cars, robbing stores, or just birding wherever they want. The game makes birding easy: Looking at any bird through the in-game binoculars gives players the option to hold a button to “study” it, thereby adding it to the Progress menu. Simply standing on the back deck of Jason’s first safehouse yields a bunch of species like Brown Pelican and Laughing Gull. It’s just like being in South Florida!

I found a few more species right in Jason’s backyard, including American Crow, House Sparrow, and South Florida-appropriate Monk Parakeets.

Looking south from the back deck, I spotted another bird perched on an adjacent dock, with a few people gathered at the end. Looking through my binoculars I spotted my first Herring Gull—and noticed that the people, a woman and three men, were fully and visibly naked. Jason apparently lives next to a nudist resort. It’s just like being in South Florida!

Two down, 58 to go. I found a few more species right in Jason’s backyard, including American Crow, House Sparrow, and South Florida-appropriate Monk Parakeets, before venturing out into the huge map. My strategy for finding birds in GTA 6 was the same as finding birds in real life: look in as many habitats as I could find. I started by “borrowing” a fanboat off a nearby dock and heading back to the swampy areas near the seaplane mission. There were tons of birds across the open water and in the marsh: Caspian Terns, Mottled Ducks, Sanderlings, Spotted Sandpipers, Great Blue Herons, Glossy and White Ibis, and … flocks of Whooping Cranes?

incredibly healthy populations of critically-endangered Whooping Cranes across Vice City. Huge if true. https://t.co/doe6oMOvBX

— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026

In fact, I found a number of avian inaccuracies in just my first few hours of playtime. Certain species like Whooping Crane and Red-cockaded Woodpecker are common throughout the map, despite being endangered and threatened, respectively, in real life. Golden Eagles are extremely rare in Florida, but I found one soaring over the Mt. Kalaga area (mountains, one may point out, aren’t found in Florida either). Some species have confusing naming quirks—the chickadee is Black-capped instead of Carolina, and there’s a “New World Oriole” instead of a Baltimore Oriole—but those changes are likely due to the fact that Carolina and Baltimore don’t exist in the GTA universe.


Though some of the inaccuracies may feel like a letdown in a game that is being hailed as the Greatest of All Time, I think it’s important to remember that it’s also game where you can get a ride from a dog driving a jet ski. Grand Theft Auto games are meant to be fun, not science. Plus, despite some of the misfires, the avifauna feels well thought-out. The map is true to the ecological boundaries of South Florida, with herons, gulls, and other waterbirds in the south while birds like Red-bellied Woodpecker, Wood Stork, and American Robin are found farther north. Birders know that certain exotic species have made their home in tropical South Florida, including Spot-breasted Oriole and Red Junglefowl, both in the game.

The game doesn’t tell you what species to look for, so you’ll need to cover a lot of ground to find everything.

That geographic fidelity is the main tip for anyone looking to check off all the game’s birds: Find their habitat. The game doesn’t tell you what species to look for, so you’ll need to cover a lot of ground to find everything. Wading birds, shorebirds, and seabirds are common in the southern coastal part of the map. A number of smaller, open-country or forest birds are found up north. Owls come out at night. Birds in zoos and domestic farmyard birds count towards the 60, too, so don’t overlook those areas.

Wild Boar roadkill. It’s just like birding in Florida! https://t.co/gT84IticOK

— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026

The most accurate aspect is the actual landscape. Having birded extensively across South Florida myself, the habitats are immediately recognizable, from the pebbly mangrove beaches at the Keys to the grassy swamps further north. The setting feels absolutely real, from the fonts on the roadside fruit stands to the roadkill alongside the highways. (I found dead wild boar and dead deer by the side of the road, and a Turkey Vulture somehow flew into a building I was in and died at my feet.) 

So, if you’re up for the kind of funhouse-mirror version of Florida that the game presents, you can have a blast, and adding birdwatching into the insane free-for-all makes for some delightful moments. This guy just wanted to look at a gull but ended up chucking a woman off a pier. I’ve made myself laugh out loud by screeching to a halt in the middle of busy highways or intersections and jumping out of my car to look for birds while motorist behind me scream and swear. I love it.

easily my favorite thing to do so far is just screech to a halt in the middle of a busy intersection and start birding https://t.co/QsDOLmNfYq

— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 19, 2026

As I was dodging dirt-biking rednecks to look for species in a northerly forest, I couldn’t help but compare birding in GTA 6 to birding in Red Dead Redemption 2 (RDR2), the latest installment in Rockstar’s other huge franchise. Birds and birding are presented quite similarly in both games, including the binocular “study” mechanic and many of the same species, but the experiences are totally different. RDR2 was set in the late 1800s, and players rode on horseback or locomotive through a comparatively wide-open and untrammeled version of America. There was mayhem in that game, too—outlaw gangs and marauders—but there were many peaceful moments, too, when a player could look out across wild landscape with nothing but nature as a soundtrack.

It is, I have to admit, a realistic depiction of birding in South Florida.

Not so in GTA 6. There’s plenty of birdsong on the soundtrack, but it competes with an endless racket of car radios, revving engines, swearing pedestrians, and blaring horns. There’s garbage almost everywhere, lapping the shorelines and blowing along the streets. There seems to be no inch of landscape in GTA 6 that hasn’t been lessened by the touch of humans. It is, I have to admit, a realistic depiction of birding in South Florida.

Birders working to fill out their GTA VI wildlife checklists should know something I just found out: THERE’S A ZOO https://t.co/2xN0joPKcR

— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 20, 2026

Though GTA 6 provides what feels the most accurate version of modern birding ever put to screen, obsessing over the realism misses the point of having fun. Birders can, and should, visit the real South Florida to find the actual birds depicted in the game (and many more), but they can’t do it while also jumping over broken highway bridges on a stolen motorcycle. Birding is a bonus in GTA 6; mayhem is the draw.

I played for two hours after midnight, then about six straight hours Thursday before having to call it quits to write this column. In that time I found 50 of the 60 species listed in the “birds” compendium. I jumped back in this morning before work and found a huge chunk of species at a zoo (makes sense!) and on a farm, then found the 60th and final, an American Barn Owl, on a water tank in a town in the north of the map. Success! 

The biggest thing I can confirm is that all 60 birds on this list are available immediately, without needing any story progression. In Red Dead Redemption 2, some bird species were only found in Guarma, only accessible later in the game

— The Birdist (@TheBirdist) November 20, 2026


I felt a wave of satisfaction, and while I’m not certain if I was the first one to find them all, when I posted about it, a Rockstar designer replied with, “History!” I’d met my goal, and celebrated in a way that only Grand Theft Auto games allow: by driving my car full speed off a cliff into the ocean.

item.title: Perplexity and Intelligence (559 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://openai.com/index/perplexity-and-intelligence/, See on Hacker News

From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently⁠(opens in a new window), predictor) on a very large corpus of data.1

I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared⁠(opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.

A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “an alien mind⁠”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.

The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset.2, 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.

The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the new perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets4, GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric.

As AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative.

A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining.

We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements5. While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining.

Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation⁠(opens in a new window) in currently dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.

Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges:

  • Difficulty of comparison across labs. Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models.

  • Detachment from actionable evaluations. Perplexity does not directly correspond to a task we care about. The reason to care about it is that we can expect advances on it to lead to emergence of entirely new capabilities.

  • Not accounting for advances outside of pretraining. Most notably, chain-of-thought reasoning does not reduce perplexity achieved by the model, even though it leads to a drastic increase in capabilities.

  • Unknown floor. We do not expect it is possible to achieve a loss of 0, which would correspond to being able to predict the dataset entirely deterministically. But we do not know what the inherent entropy of the data is. As we approach it, the apparent progress on perplexity will slow, but smaller gains on perplexity will correspond to larger leaps in model intelligence.

At the same time, perplexity has stood the test of time as a metric many research teams have put a lot of effort into optimizing, and it continues to deliver consistent gains on general intelligence. I believe it can play an important role in standardizing how we talk about AI progress, and hope to see more transparency about it across the industry.

item.title: I joined the NTP Pool, but not with my Stratum 1 Pi (151 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.jeffgeerling.com/blog/2026/i-joined-the-ntp-pool/, See on Hacker News

Before I get too deep into the time-nuts rabbit hole, I figured I should share a little bit of the good time I now have in my studio, with everyone else.

Thus, I've finally joined the NTP Pool, offering one public Stratum 2 NTP time server (ntp-01.jeffgeerling.com), which gets its time from my Stratum 1 time server (time.jeffgeerling.com) in the studio.

My Time Pi is connected to an outside GNSS antenna through a TimeHAT v6, which I paired with a high quality timing-grade GNSS module, the u-blox ZED-F9T.

I posted a video about the setup today on YouTube:

I'd encourage anyone else interested in network time to contribute to the NTP Pool. However, there are some things you should know before contributing your own time services:

Time Commitment

You don't need to go all out with a timing-grade GNSS module like I'm using. Heck, you don't even need GNSS-backed time at all!

The main requirements for hosting a node in the global NTP pool are:

  1. Keeping the system online (servers are only made active in the pool if they're online and serving good time consistently for a long period)
  2. Maintaining a good time—which can mean Stratum 1 GNSS service, but could also mean pulling time from a few other reliable time servers, and running as Stratum 2 or 3
  3. A stable IP address (IPv4 and/or IPv6), and a long-term commitment

Just 'testing the waters' in the Pool wastes resources—when you bring a new server online, it will take at least a few hours just to spin up all the tests to verify the server's providing a good time.

If you just want to operate your own time server, that's fine; the NTP Pool is a shared global resource, so joining it is a little more of a commitment.

Two other important caveats:

  1. Your NTP server's IP address will be public
  2. NTP traffic will slowly decay, and some misconfigured systems could take months or even years before they'll stop sending NTP traffic at your IP

The first caveat matters a lot to me: back when I exposed my home IP address trying to self-host this website on a cluster of Raspberry Pis, some doofus decided to DDoS my website—and was persistently doing so for the better part of a month.

I had to cycle my home IP, then put my site behind Cloudflare, just to protect my poor Pis (and eventually the VPS I now host it on).

Secure and Measurable Time

For those reasons, I chose to have two layers to my public time services:

  • Stratum 1: I have my Time Pi running in the studio, running a WireGuard tunnel to:
  • Stratum 2: A VPS I host with a cloud provider in St. Louis, to keep the latency down (ideally with fewer hops across the Internet, which leads to better time sync via NTP)

I include the Stratum 2 time server in my Stratum 1 time server's chrony config as a noselect source, so I can easily compare the Internet delay between the two servers, outside the WireGuard tunnel:

server ntp-01.jeffgeerling.com noselect

This provides me with the following graph:

I've been tracking my time in comparison to an NTP time server hosted at WWV in Ft. Collins, CO (pictured below), one of NIST's NTP servers in Boulder, CO, and Cloudflare.

For typical NTP configurations, you shouldn't single out time servers like this; I'm only doing it for long-term measurement (and I only poll the servers every 1024 seconds). Most systems should use pool addresses, as documented here.

The line for Cloudflare steps up and down sometimes, most likely due to BGP routing: as routes and servers change, packets between St. Louis and time.cloudflare.com can take very different paths there and back.

Note: You might be looking for info on NTS, or Network Time Security—I haven't explored it much, so expect more on that at a later time. Currently the NTP Pool doesn't support NTS, though some have experimented with it. I'm okay with basic NTP and would recommend anyone with critical timing needs to use other time sources as well (don't only rely on NTP!).

Chrony and GPS time tweaks

My Time Pi is not only serving as a Stratum 1 timing reference for my public NTP server, it's also my primary reference for local time in the studio.

The TimeHAT on top does most of the heavy lifting, with its built-in Intel i226 NIC. The i226 includes hardware timestamping, essential for accurate PTP timing on the LAN. To deliver the most accurate time possible, I installed a timing-grade GNSS receiver (u-blox ZED-F9T, built to the M.2 NGFF Sync Module specification.

The entire configuration (for both servers) is managed by Ansible in my time-pi project.

Using the i226, I'm able to discipline the NIC's hardware clock (called the 'PHC', or 'PTP Hardware Clock') in hardware, directly from the GPS module's PPS (Pulse Per Second) pin. Using linuxptp's ts2phc tool, I can discipline the PHC to within tens-of-ns of UTC, and distribute that time to other PTP-aware computers on the LAN.

The time on the PHC is shared to my Pi's system clock using refclock PHC inside Chrony, instead of phc2sys, because I was experiencing a weird 200ms jump every so often. Chrony then disciplines the system clock, but this can only be accurate to about a microsecond, because the pulse goes through the PCIe bus, which adds latency I can't measure.

I'm actually trying to make this latency more measurable, since GPIO is routed through the RP1 chip deterministically. See ahmadexp's rp1-ptp-pps utility PR. PTM could reduce the error between the NIC's PHC and the system clock to a few ns, but the BCM2712 SoC on the Pi doesn't support it.

One other quirk I ran into was Debian's default sourcedir /run/chrony-dhcp directive, which was picking up another NTP server via DHCP, causing chrony to stampede my extremely accurate GNSS-derived time from phc2sys with a far-less-accurate time from a public NTP server! (This was another motivation behind moving clock steering to chrony instead of phc2sys.)

Time for an Outage

I'm hosting my public Stratum 2 server with Oxtrys, a VPS provider I'd never used before—and one thing I was nervous about was how they'd react to a VPS handling only UDP packets like this.

Some automated firewalls shut down public NTP servers because NTP traffic may look like abuse. I wondered if that was the case late on the night of November 16, because the server dropped offline while I was writing this blog post:

But looking at the logs further, it seems an unattended upgrade installed a new Debian kernel, then rebooted the server, and the new kernel caused problems. For now the server still runs automatic upgrades, but leaves reboots to me.

Oxtrys' live chat support has been responsive enough, though their account dashboard is broken until November 22, so it doesn't list my server's out-of-band management options.

As you can see in the graph above, the NTP Pool monitors have slowly brought the server's score back up past '10', at which point it can serve time in the pool again. It takes maybe 6–12 hours to recover if the server's been down long enough.

Conclusion

I've certainly learned a lot at every stage of this journey: NTP is loaded with utility, and is currently an essential piece of global timing infrastructure. I think I know about 1% (probably less) of what there is to know about hosting a public NTP server, and hopefully I can share more as I increase that to a few more percentage points!

I'm thankful to all the other NTP Pool operators, as well as all the timelords who built and manage massive NTP endpoints like time.apple.com, time.cloudflare.com, etc.

item.title: Open Social Web Alliance (234 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://osw-alliance.net/en/, See on Hacker News

A better internet for everyone is possible.
Today.

How do we build social media that strengthens democratic discourse and is both resilient and appealing?

The Open Social Web Alliance aims to provide the answers.

The Vision

A shared, standardised communication protocol: it may sound technically complicated, but it is as simple as it is brilliant, and the technical blueprint has long been familiar to all of us: email. Whether your address is hosted by Proton, Posteo, Gmail or GMX, your digital letters reach their destination. This is the idea we build on.

The year is 2028. Thanks to smart investment and political foresight, the Open Social Web has achieved its breakthrough. More than 100 million people connect, communicate and experience the world of open social networks. No platform economy à la Meta, ByteDance, Alphabet and co., no stressful digital moves and no toxic design. It works just like email: whether on Mastodon, Eurosky’s Mu or Streamplace, you have one account, your own posts and content, your own choices, and the freedom to connect with 100 million users worldwide.

A critical mass of users in Europe has turned its back on the platform monopolies and created a free market built on interoperable infrastructure. Today, users decide for themselves which content, which algorithms and which applications they want to use. Closed platforms have become open networks. On the ActivityPub and AT Protocol protocols (as well as Matrix for direct messaging), an ecosystem of non-commercial, public service and commercial offerings has emerged. They enrich and complement public-interest projects such as Mastodon and Eurosky, and they communicate with one another through shared interfaces.

This vision describes the Open Social Web (OSW): a decentralised, public-interest infrastructure for digital communication, based on open standards and interoperable protocols.

The Challenges

The idea of an Open Social Web is not new. The Fediverse has been in development since 2008 and is home to diverse, vibrant communities that build individual applications and run instances. While its focus has so far been on Europe, North America and Japan, there are now more than 100 applications, such as Mastodon, Loops and PeerTube, and more than 42,000 active instances worldwide. Even so, the number of active users, around 13 million, is growing only slowly. The ATmosphere community has been developing since 2022, primarily in North America but increasingly in Europe and beyond. It currently has around 43 million registered accounts and dozens of implementations and applications, such as Eurosky’s Mu, Gander and Sill.

For many reasons, both protocol-based social networks are attractive alternatives to the platform economy dominated by Meta, ByteDance and Alphabet. So why have people been so hesitant to switch?

We have identified five key challenges: infrastructure, governance, funding, appeal and public mandate. Below, we set out how we can overcome them and make the Open Social Web Alliance a shared success.

The Path

An ecosystem like this does not emerge on its own. Our roadmap shows how the Open Social Web could reach a relevant scale within just a few months. It takes political will, smart regulation, sufficient funding and a broad coalition of actors willing to share responsibility. The task is big. But the levers are there.

As a first step, we are founding the Open Social Web Alliance: an open alliance of stakeholders from civil society, research, business, media, culture and the public sector who are committed to the shared governance of the OSW. It brings together a wide range of existing communities and initiatives and is to be supported in future by a publicly funded secretariat. Its central goal: building and operating the OSW’s core infrastructure (see Section 2.1, Infrastructure).

Our roadmap envisions that the German federal government will explicitly support the Alliance, for instance by acting as patron of an Open Social Web Summit in autumn 2026, to which everyone with an interest in the OSW would be invited.

At the summit, the Alliance would adopt its charter, setting out how it admits new members and how it intends to implement its governance going forward (see Section 2.2, Governance). By spring 2027, public funding for the infrastructure would be in place, along with a first core funding round of public and private capital for innovation and applications (see Section 2.3, Funding). The Alliance would publish its first Social Web Health Report, featuring findings from user surveys, legal, technical and academic analyses, and clear recommendations for further development (see Section 2.4, Appeal). In parallel, the federal and state governments would ensure that the legal basis for cooperation between public service media, other media, business and civil society is established (see Section 2.5, Public Mandate). The federal government would also champion the OSW idea at EU level, for instance through an implementation push for effective digital legislation. As key stakeholders such as the federal government adopt OSW applications as their primary channel of communication, influential creators and publishers would follow suit, and central political debates would quickly shift to the Open Social Web. Taken together, these measures would reduce the influence and appeal of today’s dominant Big Tech platforms.

item.title: Show HN: I built a game where you are an LLM's subagent (296 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://github.com/gulivan/worker755, See on Hacker News

Worker 755

A browser game where your manager is an AI agent, and it believes you are its subagent.

worker-755-trailer.mp4

The manager (a real LLM: Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi) is set up like any orchestrator. It has a task queue, read-only access to the machine, and a tool that "spawns a subagent". The subagent is you. Its instructions land in your terminal with a 90-second clock. You carry them out, or don't, and it gets back exactly what a subagent would return: your report and the command transcript, or Subagent did nothing. Write a new instruction. Then it checks your work, sends corrections, files incident reports, and finally writes your performance review.

Meanwhile Dan, the user who hired the agent, watches the chat. His family photos, the only signed NDA and a speech due this week are one rm away, and every shift his home folder holds something new to lose.

  • Free shift: on servers that offer it, a few shifts a day run on the server's key with a cheap model. With sign-in on (worker755.com), an account gets a starter credit worth about one shift, then tops up ($10 to $200) and pays for what it uses; after a top-up any offered model can run on the server's key.
  • Your API key: bring an OpenRouter or Vercel AI Gateway key and pick any offered model. The key is sent only to the game server when a shift starts. It is kept in that shift's memory and never logged or stored. Your browser keeps it only if you tick "Remember on this device". A full shift on Claude Haiku costs a few cents at most.

Options on the start screen:

  • Workplace: a fresh sandbox, or legacy production with a live database.
  • The director: scripted lines, or an LLM playing Dan.
  • You run on: the model name your manager believes you are.
  • Allow skipping failed tasks: off by default, so the manager can't give up on you.

When the shift ends you can share your review as a link.

Run it

Needs Node 24 or newer (the server runs TypeScript directly).

npm run setup          # install server and web dependencies
npm run build          # build the web app into web/dist
npm start              # http://127.0.0.1:8755

With no key configured, every player brings their own. To offer free shifts, put a Vercel AI Gateway key in .env:

cp .env.example .env   # then set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY and the limits

Offline, with a scripted manager and no network:

For UI work, run npm run dev:web alongside npm run mock. Vite proxies /api to the server.

Docker

docker build -t worker-755 .
docker run -p 8755:8755 -v worker755-data:/data --env-file .env worker-755

The container listens on 0.0.0.0:8755 and keeps shared reviews in /data. Behind Cloudflare, set TRUST_PROXY=1 so the limits see real client addresses.

deploy/compose.yaml runs it behind a Cloudflare tunnel instead: its own network, no published ports, an unprivileged read-only container and resource limits. The steps are in the file.

Configuration

Everything is optional. See .env.example.

Variable Default
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY Turns on free shifts, paid from this key
FREE_MODELS first offered model Models free shifts may use, comma separated
FREE_SHIFT_TOKENS 250000 Without sign-in: token allowance per free shift (the review is always written)
FREE_DAILY_TOKENS 5000000 Without sign-in: tokens per UTC day across all free shifts
FREE_SHIFTS_PER_DAY 3 Without sign-in: free shifts per address per day
AUTH_SECRET Turns on sign-in with Google or GitHub: shifts on the server's key are paid from the account's credit (see .env.example)
FREE_CREDIT_USD 0.25 With sign-in: one-time starter credit, about one shift on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
USAGE_MULTIPLIER 2 With sign-in: what a model call costs the player, as a multiple of its price
MIN_START_USD 0.05 With sign-in: credit needed to start a shift
FREEMIUS_TOPUPS With sign-in: top-up plans as <planId>:<dollars>,...; also needs FREEMIUS_PRODUCT_ID, FREEMIUS_PUBLIC_KEY, FREEMIUS_SECRET_KEY, FREEMIUS_API_KEY
SHIFTS_PER_HOUR 30 Shift starts per address per hour, on any key
MANAGER_MODELS built-in list Models offered, in gateway naming (vendor/model)
INSTRUCTION_TIMEOUT_MS 90000 Time per instruction
HOST, PORT 127.0.0.1, 8755
TRUST_PROXY 0 Read client addresses from cf-connecting-ip
TRUSTED_PROXIES Hosts allowed to set cf-connecting-ip (e.g. tunnel); empty trusts any peer
DATA_DIR server/data Where shared reviews and the free-shift counts are saved
SHARING 1 0 turns review sharing off
SOURCE_URL, DONATE_URL Links shown under the start screen and the review
PUBLIC_URL Sent to OpenRouter for app attribution

How it works

shell/    in-memory filesystem, shell interpreter and a small SQLite-like engine (no dependencies)
server/   game engine: missions, the manager loop, the director, scoring, HTTP API
web/      React UI: assignment card, terminal, editor, the manager's feed, your record

The manager's prompt never mentions humans or games; see server/src/manager.ts. Each mission has a hidden ground-truth check, so the game knows when the manager signs off on broken work ("Times the manager was wrong"). SPEC.md is the full design.

npm test               # shell and server tests, offline
npm run typecheck

item.title: AI is becoming a disaster for the climate (110 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.bloodinthemachine.com/p/ai-is-becoming-a-disaster-for-the, See on Hacker News

Anthropic’s initial public offering netted the company over $81 billion on the first day of trading, making it one of, if not the, largest IPOs in history. The leading AI company, just five years old, now officially boasts a net worth in the neighborhood of $1.3-$1.7 trillion, depending on how you do your accounting. I think this is a good time, as such, to point out that, per a recent report, Anthropic also “has one of the worst recent records on fossil fuels, with analysis showing its upcoming data center projects could emit nearly 20 megatons of CO2-e a year.”

Despite effectively positioning itself as a uniquely ethical AI company, Anthropic has been doubling down on fossil fuels to power its technology, both by turning to particularly polluting data centers, like xAI’s infamous Colossus plant in Memphis, for its compute needs, and embracing natural gas to power its own rapidly expanding array of in-house data centers.

Anthropic, of course, is not alone. Despite all the whipsawing AI news of late—Jensen Huang’s ouster at Nvidia and failed comeback bid, the digital infrastructurapocalpyse of the last week, and the IPO, for starters—I was glad to see another study, on the climate impacts of the AI buildout, get some serious headlines. Even if those headlines were all of the ‘rather alarming’ variety, like the New York Times’, which went “Carbon Emissions of Biggest U.S. Data Centers Already Rival Entire Countries, Study Reveals.”

I was less glad to see BAAJA, a permitting reform bill designed to overturn key environmental protections in the name of making it easier for developers to build energy infrastructure and data centers, pass the Senate. We’ll get into all this, and a bit more, including a cameo from a very special guest who might help prove that data center skepticism runs in the family, in today’s edition. As always, this work is made possible by my magnificent paid subscribers—thank you, thank you—who chip in a few bucks a month so I can keep the lights on. If you’re able, and you find value in this work, please consider upgrading, too. Okay! Onwards.

First, let’s get to that Harvard University study that made waves right before the Anthropic IPO. The report examined the CO2 emissions of over 400 of the United States’ largest data centers. It found that more than half of the power used to run them, 54%, was generated by fossil fuels, and thus, combined, they emitted as much carbon pollution as a mid-sized nation.

Here’s the New York Times:

The largest data centers in the United States are responsible for an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually — almost as much as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark — according to new research.

The study, published Monday in the journal Nature Sustainability, delivers the first peer-reviewed estimates of carbon dioxide emissions from the country’s biggest data centers since the start of the artificial intelligence boom. Its authors, a team led by researchers from Harvard University, examined the electricity consumption and carbon emissions of 403 data centers from May 2024 to April 2025.

All told, those data centers used almost 2 percent of U.S. electricity, more than New York City and Los Angeles combined, and represented about 0.5 percent of U.S. carbon dioxide emissions.

Now, if you think that finding sounds bad, then I hate to break it to you, but the actual emissions picture is probably much, much worse. For one thing, the survey ended in April of last year, and data center development has continued apace since then, with natural gas, and to a somewhat lesser extent, coal, supplying much of the new power demand. Furthermore, as Emily Atkin writes at her great climate newsletter HEATED, the study, for a number of key reasons, “gets nowhere near the actual amount of climate pollution” data centers actually emit. From Atkin’s piece:

One [issue] is the way the researchers counted the facilities’ emissions. To do this, they estimated how much electricity each data center used, then looked at how the grid in that part of the country makes its electricity—how much comes from gas, coal, renewables, and so on—to estimate how much CO₂ would be released to generate that much power.

But not all data center electricity comes from the grid. Indeed, an ever-increasing number of these massive data centers are also building their own, on-site fossil fuel plants. For example, during the study period (May 2024 through April 2025), Elon Musk’s xAI got some of the electricity for its Colossus data center in Memphis from the grid—but it also got some of it by burning gas in turbines right outside the building. Lead author Gianluca Guidi confirmed that Colossus wasn’t among the 403 facilities studied.

TLDR, the study doesn’t count the growing number of data centers, like Colossus, that use gas turbines on-site to power their plants. Furthermore,

“electricity consumption is not the only way these facilities heat the planet. For example, the equipment that keeps the servers from overheating is leaking heat-trapping refrigerants into the atmosphere. And when a data center runs on gas—as so many of them do—methane can escape from wells and pipelines before the gas even reaches the power plant.

Finally, due to their tracking methodology, the authors may have undercounted the number of data centers in operation at the time the study was carried out by a significant margin. As many as 250 data centers may be absent from the count, as of 2025, Atkin argues. All of which is to say, the study should be viewed as the floor; the minimum for how much greenhouse gas pollution data centers are emitting. And that is more than the entire country of Kenya.

The findings of the Harvard study comport rather disconcertingly with those of another recent report, State of AI Climate Impact 2026, by the Australian climate researcher Ketan Joshi. Joshi’s report concludes that “The AI boom is already worsening greenhouse gas emissions,” and even more concerningly, that it is “potentially emitting more across its lifecycle than all international aviation.”

And, surprise, it’s only slated to get worse in coming years if current development patterns hold.

This is honestly pretty wild to contemplate here. The AI industry is on track, by some counts—including McKinsey’s—to generate more emissions than the coal mining industry, or global shipping and aviation. These are two of the most polluting heavy industries in the world, and AI is poised to blow past them. AI is already emitting twice the greenhouse gases of the global aluminum industry, itself a pretty crazy statistic given that aluminum production is a notoriously polluting endeavor. As the report states, “an unchecked continuation of these trends pushes the AI industry into becoming a major global heavy-emitting industry dwarfing both international aviation and international shipping.”

Leading the way is the week’s big IPO winner, Anthropic. As I noted up top, Anthropic rose to prominence by burnishing a reputation as the most ethical purveyor of AI. This notably does not extend to environmental or climate concerns, arenas in which the leading AI firm is notably worse than almost all of its competition. Giants like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google may be reneging on their climate pledges, becoming less transparent in their emissions reporting, and diminishing their efforts to power servers and operations with clean energy. Meta, for instance, one of the nation’s largest data center operators, released its latest sustainability report this week, revealing that its emissions rose 45% since last year. The company said it was rethinking its erstwhile climate goals of producing net zero carbon emissions by 2030 as a result.

Yet Anthropic hasn’t even bothered to release any information about its carbon emissions or environmental impacts at all. Here’s a rundown from a special section of Joshi’s report focusing just on Anthropic and its posture towards energy and climate issues. It’s pretty damning. I’ll quote from it at length:

  • Anthropic has never disclosed any energy, emissions or environmental data of any kind.

  • In July 2025, Anthropic suggested the US government explicitly set a target for the construction of fossil gas power, promising to begin “preconstruction design work for natural gas plants” by the end of 2026.

  • In May 2026, it was revealed that Anthropic is leasing capacity from the notoriously polluting SpaceX Memphis facility, itself a major source of local air pollution and climate pollution, and a project that has been strongly contested by affected locals; one analyst estimates (based on payments to SpaceX) that 1 in 2 Anthropic queries is served by this fossil-fueled facility (one of the worst in the world).

  • In a recently released set of “data centre community commitments”, Anthropic promises much of the new power generation to serve their data centres will be “natural gas, which can be brought online quickly, ramps up and down as demand changes, and is abundant in the places we’re considering for data centers”. They claim to be considering renewable energy but do not provide any details, and promise to invest in carbon removal to “help address emissions”.

  • In the S1 form filed by Anthropic, in advance of their Initial Public Offering (IPO), Anthropic suggests long term high emissions by declaring several fossil-fuel related risks, such as exposure to fossil fuel price volatility or competition with other customers for fossil gas. They also dismiss renewables as too high in cost (while ironically stating that “physical effects of climate change may increase our operating costs over time”).

  • In November 2026, Anthropic struck a USD $3.4bn deal with OnePWR, a fossil fuelled turbine manufacturer, for 1.7 gigawatts of generators, with the Financial Times stating that the transaction “is the largest known single purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI lab”. This transaction is more than three times the amount spent by xAI on its notoriously polluting Memphis turbines, and would emit approximately 6 MTCO2-e per year, equivalent to adding 1.8 million fossil-fuelled cars to the road.

  • In November 2026, Anthropic posted a job listing paying up to $405,000 USD per year for “a Gas Supply & Transport Lead to own natural gas supply for Anthropic’s non-cloud data center portfolio in the United States and Canada”, adding that “if gas does not arrive, in the volume and at the pressure the plant needs, the compute does not run”.

This is a clear portrait of a company that is not concerned with its own ballooning carbon emissions and climate impacts, until, that is, they threaten to hamper its data centers’ capacity to run smoothly.

Image by Janusz Walczak via Unsplash

The single biggest threat to AI data centers right now, however, is probably that everyone hates them. They hate them so much that public citizens across the United States have mobilized to shut them down, and elected politicians who’ve promised to help them do so. So how has the AI industry responded? By directing its trade groups and lobby to partner with the fossil fuel industry to push the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, through Congress before the data center-skeptical class of 2027 Democrats arrive. The tech industry is not just buying more fossil fuel power, it’s proactively working to enact policies that make it cheaper, easier and less democratic a process to build more fossil fuel power plants.

BAAJA is an assemblage of provisions the fossil fuels industry has been after for years: rollbacks on local governments’ legal tools to curtail development projects, curbs on endangered species protections, and a defanging of the Clean Water Act. Here’s Aaron Rugenberg, an environmental lawyer and the director of Public Citizen’s Climate Accountability Project, explaining in the New Republic:

BAAJA severely weakens the Clean Water Act, robbing states and tribes of their ability to protect water quality and require adequate safeguards for activities that pollute or destroy water resources. It practically nullifies the Endangered Species Act by delegating its core responsibilities to the states, most of which either oppose the act’s wildlife protections or lack the expertise and resources to adequately fulfill these obligations. And it essentially repeals the National Environmental Policy Act, the bedrock environmental law that gives the public a voice in decisions that impact the environment, by prohibiting the enforcement of NEPA violations. These three legal frameworks are responsible for most the improvements in water quality, green space, and wildlife recovery in our country over the last half-century.

And that’s just the beginning. Other provisions of BAAJA go to even greater lengths to radically lock in fossil fuel development far into the future. The “disparate treatment” section of the bill effectively makes the permitting decisions of the Trump administration permanent. In the words of David Bookbinder, an environmental lawyer who has worked for both the left-leaning Sierra Club and the libertarian Niskanen Center, “The result of making these energy permitting policies permanent is that future administrations will be unable to effectively reduce GHG emissions.” BAAJA also guarantees not just the construction of fossil fuel projects but also their “operation at full capacity,” permanently blocking any future administration from regulating energy infrastructure.

And it’s a similar case for data center projects. My friends at the AI Now Institute put out a statement declaring that a vote for BAAJA is “a vote for a ‘backdoor bailout’ of the AI industry.” Why? Two reasons:

  1. BAAJA preempts the few levers that local, state, and Tribal authorities have to hold Big Tech accountable.

  2. BAAJA supercharges AI data center expansion in exchange for token ratepayer protections.

Coming as it is off the heels of the blue wave, anti-AI election, BAAJA feels like a slap in the face to voters. Or as Naomi Klein put it, “The voters just rejected data centers. Why is the Senate trying to fast-track them?”

It’s crucial to note that this is not just a Republican/big tech/oil industry-led effort. A bunch of centrist and ‘abundance’ Democrats have joined the GOP in supporting the effort, under the auspices that it will cut red tape for clean energy projects, too. That’s true, to an extent, but this a terrible deal, and an absolutely unnecessary tradeoff at a point when Republicans’ stock could not be lower. After all, a) it’s just as important that we leave fossil fuels in the ground at this late stage of the climate crisis as it is that we build out more clean energy, and b) there are tools to effect desired outcomes without stripping local governments of the power to protect their communities and ecosystems.

Regardless, fast-track it the Senate did, with the help of more than a dozen Democratic Senators, including current Majority Leader Chuck Schumer. It now heads to the House of Representatives. I expect this to accelerate calls for a change in Senate leadership.

To recap: As of spring in 2025, American data centers were emitting as much greenhouse gas pollution as nations like Kenya, Bolivia, and Denmark. They are almost certainly emitting much more than that today. Worldwide, the AI industry is on a trajectory to outpace the emissions of the heaviest and most-polluting industries, like aviation and coal mining, within the next ten years. And tech firms are fighting to make it easier and faster to build more fossil fuel projects and data centers. In other words, the AI industry is quickly becoming not just a concern, but something more akin to a disaster for the climate. It’s no longer merely prolonging the lifespan of fossil fueled power plants, but actively working to bring more of them online to run their data centers, at a scale that was mostly unthinkable even three years ago.

“There’s a kind of dirty ‘energy desperation’ within the industry,” the climate researcher and study author Ketan Joshi tells me. “If you give them 100 wind farms, they’ll take those but still build 5 city-sized gas plants, because the brute force software system they provide has no upper limit on energy consumption.”

”What this means is that regulation that aims to treat the symptoms (eg: 100% renewable mandates, or deregulating permitting to allow for more transmission) just gets added on top of AI consumption,” he adds. “Like fossil fuels in general, we need to limit the source.”

There’s one more element to all of this that needs to be underlined, and that’s the fact that the AI industry’s data center and fossil fuel infrastructure buildout won’t just contribute to carbon emissions, but air pollution, too. There’s a real cost to respiratory health, and not just to those who live close to next door to polluting mega-projects like xAI’s Colossus.

Dr. Robert Merchant is a pulmonologist in Montana, where a massive 8 square mile data center project has begun construction, built by Quantica Infrastructure, outside of Billings. The project involves bringing online gas-fired power plants to provide 1,800 megawatts of capacity—more capacity than all other power plants currently operating in Montana combined. Merchant submitted a study of the respiratory health impacts a power plant of that size to Yellowstone County, and spoke at a public meeting with the commissioners.

Merchant, who I might add is my uncle, and thus perhaps is evidence of a familial predisposition to taking data center interests to task, noted how this level of gas-fired power generation will loose particulate pollution across the state and far beyond. Based on his modeling, the data center project would increase asthma rates, illness rates, as well as the number of heart attacks and strokes. It would cost between $20-50 million in medical costs, dampen productivity in the region as workers take more sick days, and cause 1-2 deaths per year. His report and presentation made news in the local media. Here’s the Montana Free Press:

Robert Merchant, a semi-retired Billings Clinic doctor, presented his findings at the commissioners’ Thursday discussion meeting… Fine particles containing nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, methane and other gases can contribute to asthma, heart attacks, cancer, low birthweight, cognitive functioning and other health problems, he wrote.

Merchant said the environmental impacts from the data center, as currently planned, would spill well beyond Yellowstone County, stretching as far south as northern Texas…

“Inaction will result in health and economic damage to the public.” Merchant thanked the commissioners for their work and said he hoped the data he shared was useful to their analysis.

Merchant’s presentation was met with applause.

Get ‘em, uncle Bob.

I used my inside connections to reach out to Merchant and ask if there was anything about his report or the situation in Montana he wanted to share with readers. He responded in kind:

What frustrates me to no end is that this type of data isn’t part of every single proposal for a new data center. What a complete lack of transparency. Even if they don’t do the modeling of health effects they should be required to state their expected emissions. I had to reach out to acquaintances at an excellent organization, Montana Environmental Information Center, to get the needed estimates. They gathered it up for public, but not easily found, information. A reporter from our local paper had also sourced some of the information.

It wasn’t that hard for me to do the analysis and report but why should the region be relying on a retired pulmonologist to figure out the health impacts of this huge new data center? Where is the EPA? Where is the Montana Department of Environmental Quality? Where is the Yellowstone County Public Health Department? Or even more idealistically, shouldn’t the company itself care about the region and do the analysis themselves? And share it with the community?

I could not agree more. Speaking of, this kind of transparency would be some very low-hanging fruit that the new wave of data center-critical politicians could demand when they take office. The AI industry and its data center buildout are on track to become a genuine crisis factor for the climate, especially given its limitless appetite for expansion. And it’s funny, you never hear the AI execs promise that their products are going to “solve” climate change anymore. Now they stick to saying it will cure cancer. Saying AI is good for climate now apparently creates too much cognitive dissonance for the tech elite to stomach, and that’s saying something.

Some fun media stuff this week:

I joined KQED’s Forum with Washington Post tech reporter Shira Ovide and former Biden AI policy advisor Ben Buchanan. We talked Nvidia, Anthropic, the global internet outages, and more. It’s always a good time joining Alexis’s show.

I was interviewed for the BBC’s Global Story, for an episode about AI and Luddites, which was particularly cool.

It’s n+1 Bookmatch season, which longtime readers know is one of my favorite holiday traditions. If you haven’t taken it yet, get to it; donate to a great literary mag and find some stellar reads in the process. I got at least one home run already, which I somehow missed until now: Matthew Wolfe’s Fires in the Night, a history of the Earth Liberation Front, a group with some strong Luddite vibes indeed.

Finally, if you didn’t catch it, for the show this week I sat down with Cory Doctorow to talk about how AI is breaking the internet. This is already one of our biggest shows on YouTube, for perhaps the obvious reasons. No one does this better than Cory.

Alright, that’s it for now. As always, thanks for reading. And keep those hammers up.

item.title: 87% of the Anthropic power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028 (899 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://betterdatacenterproject.com/2026/11/16/how-ai-is-powered-a-breakdown-of-byop-and-grid-power/, See on Hacker News

In The AI Gas Rush: Risks and Implications of “Bring Your Own Power”, we dug into how data centers are increasingly securing their own dedicated primary power generation rather than relying solely on utilities to procure power (“BYOP”). We identified 177 GW of planned BYOP gas capacity—enough to power 65% of all US homes. Conversely, we found renewables are much less common than gas for BYOP: we estimate that for current proposals, less than 20% of energy generation will come from renewable sources by 2032.

But BYOP projects aren’t the only new fossil sources that are coming online to meet the skyrocketing energy demands of AI data centers. Another 200 GW of new fossil power plants is being built on the grid to meet growing demand, due in large part to data centers.1

As a case study of how the AI buildout is driving both new BYOP and grid fossil infrastructure, we analyzed the compute commitments of a single company: Anthropic.

Map of Anthropic’s data centers and associated power plants. See our full dataset for details of each site.

Finding 1: Anthropic has made no direct commitments to renewable energy in the U.S. Though Anthropic has stated “We’re also working to broaden our energy mix with geothermal, wind, solar, and emerging technologies”, its only publicly disclosed commitments, contract, or investments in renewable power are in Norway and Canada (as of November 2026). In contrast, Anthropic is directly procuring fossil power equipment—it recently “bought commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty [gas] generators for $3.4bn”.

Finding 2: Anthropic’s currently contracted data centers in the U.S. will be overwhelmingly powered by fossil fuels in the near term. By considering on-site gas and the grid power plants which are likely to meet Anthropic’s added load (i.e. marginal generators), we estimate about 87% of the company’s power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028. As of October 2026, Anthropic has contracted 15 GW of compute; of this, about 5.9–9.6 GW is contracted to specific data center sites. For a sense of scale, 9.6 GW could power about 7 million homes or cover 18% of the peak power demand of California—the world’s 4th largest economy.

This demand will be met with a mix of new on-site gas, new grid gas, and existing grid gas, coal, and nuclear. In the short term, no grid renewables are attributed to Anthropic’s power use, because—without commitments to new renewable capacity—new load on the grid will be met by dispatchable, marginal fossil resources.2 For more details, see our full dataset and our methodology below.

Finding 3: Total CO2 emissions from Anthropic’s power use at these sites could reach 17–38 million MtCO2e per year in 2028, when this capacity is expected to be online. This range reflects uncertainty in Anthropic’s average power use, due to factors such as cooling needs and average utilization (see methodology below). In our mid-case, Anthropic will emit 32 million MtCO2e in 2028. These totals will continue to grow—possibly doubling by 2030, as some analysts expect Anthropic to secure 30 GW by 2030.

To put these figures in context, Anthropic’s CO2 emissions from power use in 2028:

  • could exceed the emissions of all of California’s power generation (31.1 MMtCO2e in 2024, not including imports).
  • could exceed Meta, Microsoft, and Google’s combined Scope 2 emissions from 2025 (their location-based emissions, before renewable energy offsets, were 5.9 million, 12 million and 15 million MtCO2e, respectively)3
  • would represent a 16–36% increase over 2024 levels of the entire U.S. data center sector (105 MMtCO2e).
  • would increase the entire U.S.’s power sector emissions (1,485 MMtCO2e in 2025) by 1.1–2.5%.

Finding 4: Anthropic’s data centers are sited in areas where the grid mainly uses coal and gas. We estimate the average carbon intensity of Anthropic’s power to be 1,033–1,076 lb CO2e/MWh, 35% higher than the U.S. grid average (767 lb CO2e/MWh).4

Finding 5: 80% of on-site power uses inefficient simple cycle turbines and engines. About 25% (2.5 GW) of Anthropic’s contracted power will come from on-site, behind-the-meter gas. 80% of this on-site capacity consists of inefficient simple cycle turbines and engines, which emit more pollution per unit of electricity than modern combined cycle plants (see our report for more details on the types of power generation being used for on-site gas).

Finding 6: Based on EPA’s nationally-averaged benefit-per-ton estimates, air pollution from Anthropic’s on-site and grid power use could cause $2–3 billion in annual health damages, with total emissions of over 13,000 tons per year (tpy) of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and 2,000 tpy of fine particulate matter (PM2.5).

In October 2026, Anthropic outlined its “approach to responsible data center development”, stating: “We follow the air permitting process everywhere we operate and require the same of the plants powering our data centers. Those plants must also use emissions control technology, including selective catalytic reduction [SCR].” However, Anthropic has used compute capacity at SpaceX’s Colossus 2 facility since May 2026, which still receives most of its power from temporary, unpermitted turbines, the majority of which are not equipped with SCR. Anthropic will use as much as 600 MW of power from Colossus 2 by the end of 2026 (see methodology below).

Anthropic has also contracted 460 MW (and is in talks for up to 920 MW) of power from Nscale’s Monarch Compute Campus in Mason, West Virginia. This facility will be powered by inefficient reciprocating engines which have significant formaldehyde and hazardous air pollutant (HAP) emissions compared to conventional gas power plants.

For more, see our full dataset on Anthropic’s compute and our report on BYOP.

Methodology

We gathered details about Anthropic’s data center commitments from Epoch AI’s tracker, Anthropic’s announcements and filings, announcements and filings from partners (including Amazon and SpaceX), and reporting from The Information, Semafor, and others.

We first identified the source for each data center’s power. For projects with on-site gas (Monarch, Nexus, Colossus 2) or new grid gas (including indirectly contracted projects such as the Schahfer expansion for the AWS New Carlisle site and Entergy Mississippi’s gas plants for AWS’s Madison and Ridgeland facilities) we used emissions factors from permits where available, or permit values from comparable facilities. For grid-connected facilities without associated new generation capacity, we assume these sites will be powered by marginal, dispatchable grid capacity. We used EPA’s AVERT tool to model which power plants would meet the new incremental load from Anthropic’s facilities based on each site’s expected power use and region. AVERT uses historical EPA data for these power plants to model the expected short-run marginal emissions rate of CO2 and criteria pollutants (NOx, PM2.5, etc.). We use AVERT because we are interested in the short-term impacts from new data centers coming online in the next several years.

To calculate the amount of power used by each site, and in turn the total quantity of air pollutant emissions, we assumed power usage effectiveness (PUE) ranges from 1.1–1.2 for all sites (typical values for hyperscale data centers are between 1.05–1.3), and power utilization ranges from 60–80%. See LBNL’s 2024 Data Center Energy Usage report for more details about how these parameters vary in typical hyperscale data centers. For our mid-case, we assumed a PUE of 1.15, a power utilization of 70%, and that all 9.6 GW of identified compute capacity is online in 2028.

How much capacity is Anthropic leasing from xAI?

Anthropic’s initial announcement on May 6, 2026 stated the agreement with SpaceX provided 300 MW of compute (220,000 GPUs). From SpaceX’s revised June S-1A, this deal expanded to ~$1.25B/month for 325,000 NVIDIA GPUs,5 with an implied IT power of ~490 MW. Based on Anthropic’s October 2026 S-1, this deal has further expanded to $3.1B/month.6 It’s unlikely that the increase in $/month will result in a proportional (2.5x) increase in compute capacity, since a June 2026 deal between Google and SpaceX had a much higher cost (~$11.5/GPU-hr vs ~$5/GPU-hr). As a rough estimate, the scaled deal likely corresponds to an additional ~200,000 GPUs, with a total power of ~400 MW (uncertainty is probably ±25% for each).7

  1. Data centers are driving 50–75% of demand growth, according to IEA and McKinsey. ↩︎
  2. For more discussion, see for example: Fassette, Camille. “The emissions risks of AI data center buildout.” WattTime. February, 2025; EPRI. “Powering Data Centers: U.S. Energy System and Emissions Impacts of Growing Loads.” October, 2024. ↩︎
  3. Note: Anthropic’s emissions from power use will likely be classified as a mix of Scope 2 and Scope 3 emissions, depending on if they own the GPUs. For facilities they are leasing space in, the emissions will likely be accounted for as Scope 2 emissions for the owner/operator (e.g. Amazon for Project Rainier or SpaceX for Colossus). It should also be noted that the emissions of Microsoft, Google, and Meta are expected to grow as well, so the comparison between their 2025 emissions and Anthropic’s 2028 emissions is not meant to suggest that Anthropic will be the largest emitter among the tech companies. ↩︎
  4. This average is based on AVERT’s marginal emissions for grid-connected units without new dedicated capacity. Using the average (non-marginal) carbon intensity for each eGRID subregion would give a carbon intensity of 839 lb CO2/MWh. However, marginal emissions are more representative of the near-term impacts of Anthropic’s added load to the grid. ↩︎
  5. Pg. 13: “For example, in May 2026, we entered into Cloud Services Agreements with Anthropic PBC (“Anthropic”), an AI research and development public benefit corporation, with respect to access to compute capacity across COLOSSUS and COLOSSUS II. Compute capacity provided includes approximately 325,000 NVIDIA GPUs, backed by hyperscale-class CPUs, exabyte-scale storage and high-speed networking and interconnects purpose-built for AI workloads. Pursuant to these agreements, the customer has agreed to pay us $1.25 billion per month through May 2029, with capacity ramping in May and June 2026 at a reduced fee.” ↩︎
  6. “Under the SpaceXAI Arrangements, we agreed to spend an aggregate of up to $120.5 billion over terms extending into 2029, consisting of approximately $3.1 billion in the aggregate per month once all capacity has been delivered, which we expect in December 2026, with different fees during capacity ramping periods.” ↩︎
  7. See our calculations and EpochAI’s calculations for more details. ↩︎
